openingProblem.problem: In December 1981 the Polish army crushed Solidarity with Soviet encouragement. In 1989 Solidarity won an election and every Communist regime in Eastern Europe fell, while the Soviet army stayed in its barracks. What changed between 1981 and 1989?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: why did Moscow use force in 1981 but not in 1989?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: Living on borrowed time: debt and decline
chunks.body:
By 1981 Eastern Europe's Communist regimes were in deep economic trouble. In the 1970s Western banks had lent freely to the Soviet bloc, reassured by the stability that the Red Army seemed to guarantee. Governments used the money to buy Western goods and to subsidise food and consumer prices, avoiding the unpopular reforms their economists recommended. Tony Judt's figures show the scale. Eastern Europe's hard-currency debt rose from $6.1 billion in 1971 to $66.1 billion in 1980, and would reach $95.6 billion by 1988. Poland's debt rose from $1 billion to $20.5 billion between 1971 and 1980. In its last years East Germany spent over 60 per cent of its export earnings just on interest. The system, Judt writes, was "living not just on loans but on borrowed time".

Poland showed what happened when the bills came due. When the government raised food prices in 1976, riots forced it to back down. When it raised meat prices again on 1 July 1980, strikes spread across the country to the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk, where workers led by **Lech Wałęsa** formed an independent union, **Solidarity**. The regime gave way: on 10 November 1980 Solidarity became the first officially registered independent trade union in a Communist country, with an estimated ten million members.

Solidarity's leaders knew the history of 1956 and 1968. Soviet tanks had crushed protest in East Berlin, Hungary and Czechoslovakia. Their advisers therefore called for a "self-limiting revolution": the union accepted the Party's "leading role" and avoided foreign policy, to give Warsaw and Moscow no excuse to send in the tanks.

But the crisis deepened in 1981. Industrial productivity collapsed as newly unionised workers held meetings, protests and strikes. Seen from Moscow, Judt writes, the Polish regime was losing control and setting a dangerous example to its neighbours.

This mattered because economic failure created opposition that Communist regimes could neither satisfy nor easily repress, which meant that the Soviet Union faced a crisis in its most important satellite at the start of the 1980s.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Debt made the bloc's economies unsustainable.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Regimes chose debt to avoid unrest, which bought them time.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Price rises in Poland produced mass opposition.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Earlier protests in 1970 and 1976 had been contained.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Solidarity's self-limitation reflected fear of Soviet intervention.

howItGetsAsked: To what extent were economic problems the main cause of the crisis in Soviet control of Eastern Europe between 1981 and 1989?

useItInAnEssay.claim: Economic problems were the root of the crisis in Eastern Europe because they produced opposition the regimes could not satisfy.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Eastern Europe's hard-currency debt rose from $6.1 billion in 1971 to $66.1 billion in 1980, and when Poland raised meat prices in July 1980 strikes produced Solidarity, with ten million members.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that regimes that had bought peace with Western loans now faced organised workers, so by 1981 Poland's government was losing control.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, economic failure alone had not brought down Communist regimes before, because Soviet force had always been the final guarantee.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Economic problems were therefore the root of the crisis, while Soviet willingness to use force decided its outcome.

chunks.title: Martial law and stalemate, 1981–1985
chunks.body:
In 1981 the Polish army took charge. General **Wojciech Jaruzelski** became Prime Minister in February and Party leader in October. With the army behind him and the Soviet leadership encouraging firm action, he declared **martial law** on **13 December 1981**. Solidarity's leaders were imprisoned; the union was banned the following year and went underground.

Why did the Polish army act rather than the Soviet army? Jaruzelski claimed he was forestalling a Soviet invasion. The Office of the Historian notes that Soviet military planners were closely involved in the Polish planning for martial law, and the Warsaw Pact had long been used to contain dissent in the bloc. Moscow was also by then fighting a costly war in Afghanistan. Either way, the outcome was the same as in 1956 and 1968: the protest movement was crushed, but this time by Polish forces.

The West's response was divided. President Reagan imposed further economic sanctions on Moscow and curtailed academic exchanges. Western European governments were more cautious: Judt notes that Chancellor Helmut Schmidt's first response was to send a personal representative to Warsaw to help overcome Poland's "isolation", and that Western European opinion was more troubled by Reagan's rhetoric than by repression in Warsaw.

Martial law solved nothing. It lasted until July 1983, and Judt observes that no other Communist state had ever been driven to such measures. Society and state remained in a stand-off. In 1984 the political police murdered a popular radical priest, Jerzy Popiełuszko; his funeral drew a crowd of 350,000, revealing the scale of support for the Church and the outlawed Solidarity. Meanwhile the economy continued to sink: by the mid-1980s Poland's national debt was approaching $40 billion.

This mattered because martial law showed that the old methods could still suppress opposition but could no longer solve the bloc's problems, which meant that by the mid-1980s Communist rule in Poland rested on force alone.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Martial law crushed Solidarity without Soviet troops.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Soviet planners were closely involved (Office of the Historian).

argumentsThatWork.claim: The West was divided in its response.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Reagan's sanctions showed US support for Solidarity.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Repression could not end the stand-off between state and society.

chunks.title: Gorbachev and the end of the Brezhnev Doctrine, 1985–1988
chunks.body:
When **Mikhail Gorbachev** came to power in 1985, the Soviet Union's relationship with Eastern Europe began to change fundamentally.

The first reason was the lesson of Afghanistan. Judt writes that the war "excluded for the foreseeable future any further deployment of the Red Army beyond its frontiers". As Politburo member Yegor Ligachev later admitted, after Afghanistan "there could no longer be any question of applying force in Eastern Europe".

The second was Gorbachev's own policy. His reforms at home, perestroika and glasnost, legitimised calls for reform in the satellite states too. In Poland, Jaruzelski released Adam Michnik and other Solidarity leaders in 1986 and offered modest economic reforms, partly to attract new Western loans for a debt approaching $40 billion. In 1987 the Polish government even asked the public which price rises it would prefer; the answer was, in effect, none.

Most importantly, Gorbachev made clear, first secretly to the Eastern European leaders and then increasingly in public, that the Soviet Union had abandoned the **Brezhnev Doctrine**, the policy of military intervention to keep Communist regimes in power. The decisive public statement came in a speech to the United Nations on **7 December 1988**. Gorbachev announced unilateral cuts in Soviet conventional forces in Europe and declared: "Freedom of choice is a universal principle. There should be no exceptions." Judt argues that this was more than a renunciation of the Brezhnev Doctrine: it was understood immediately as a concession that the peoples of the satellite states were free to go their own way, socialist or not. "Eastern Europe," Judt writes, "was about to re-enter history."

The Warsaw Pact, through which Moscow had controlled its allies, was by then weakened by economic slowdown in all its members; by the late 1980s it was virtually ineffectual.

This mattered because the threat of Soviet force had always been the final guarantee of Communist rule in Eastern Europe, which meant that once Gorbachev withdrew it, the regimes had to survive on their own.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Moscow had still encouraged martial law in 1981.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Eastern European regimes tried to reform from above first.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Gorbachev hoped reformed socialism would survive.

chunks.title: 1989: the satellites go their own way
chunks.body:
In 1989 the regimes of Eastern Europe fell one after another. **Poland** led. Round Table talks between the government and Solidarity began on 6 February; the agreement of 4 April allowed free elections for 35 per cent of the lower house (the Sejm) and for a new Senate, and recognised Solidarity. On 4 June Solidarity won a crushing victory, and by 24 August Tadeusz Mazowiecki was the first non-Communist Prime Minister in Eastern Europe.

**Hungary**, already the most liberal regime, removed its veteran leader János Kádár, allowed free association and opened its border with the West, giving thousands of East Germans an escape route. On 16 June it ceremonially reburied Imre Nagy, the reforming leader executed after 1956, and on 23 October it adopted a constitution allowing multi-party elections.

**East Germany** collapsed next. As East Germans fled through Hungary and sought refuge in West German embassies, Gorbachev visited Berlin in early October and warned the leadership of the need to reform. Two weeks later Erich Honecker was forced to resign, and on **9 November 1989** the Berlin Wall came down. In **Czechoslovakia** a non-Communist government took office on 5 December, and the dissident playwright Václav Havel was elected President on 29 December. In **Bulgaria** the long-time leader Todor Zhivkov was removed. Only in **Romania** was there bloodshed: Nicolae Ceauşescu refused reform, his security forces fired on crowds, and he and his wife were executed on 25 December.

Why was this a crisis for the USSR, and why did Moscow not intervene? The Soviet Union had crushed protest in 1953, 1956 and 1968, and in 1981 it had encouraged martial law. In 1989 it stood back, because Gorbachev had abandoned the Brezhnev Doctrine and because, after Afghanistan, force was no longer an option. The West played a limited role: Judt writes that "the US played a remarkably small part in the dramas of 1989, at least until after the fact", although Solidarity had been largely financed from the US.

This mattered because the Soviet empire in Eastern Europe ended without the Soviet army firing a shot, which meant that the central division of the Cold War in Europe disappeared within a single year.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Poland's negotiated transition showed the way.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Round Table at first limited free elections to part of the Sejm.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Revolutions spread rapidly across the bloc.
Soviet restraint, not Western pressure, decided the outcome.

howItGetsAsked: Compare and contrast the Soviet response to the Polish crisis of 1981 and to the revolutions of 1989.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The Soviet response in 1989 differed fundamentally from 1981, because Moscow no longer backed the use of force.
useItInAnEssay.prove: In 1981 the Soviet leadership encouraged Jaruzelski's martial law, whereas in 1989 Gorbachev stood back as Solidarity won the elections of 4 June and the Berlin Wall fell on 9 November.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the regimes lost their final guarantee, so they negotiated, as in Poland and Hungary, or collapsed, as in East Germany and Czechoslovakia.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the underlying problems, debt and economic failure, were the same in both years, so what changed was Soviet policy, not the regimes' weakness.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The decisive difference was therefore Moscow's abandonment of force, which turned a crisis that could be suppressed into one that ended Soviet control.

modelPlan.thesis: Martial law showed that Moscow could still have opposition crushed without sending its own army, but it also revealed weakness: no other Communist state had been driven to such measures, and repression produced only a stand-off.

arguments.claim: For: Solidarity crushed without Soviet troops.
For: Soviet involvement in the planning.
Against: martial law as an admission of failure.

modelPlan.counter: Moscow's reluctance to send its own troops may itself show that its control was weakening.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Did martial law solve the crisis? No: by 1986 the regime was releasing Solidarity leaders to win Western loans.

segments.text: Martial law showed both the strength and the limits of Soviet control.

On 13 December 1981 Jaruzelski, with Soviet encouragement, imprisoned Solidarity's leaders, but martial law lasted until July 1983 and Judt notes no other Communist state had been driven to such measures.
This meant that opposition could still be crushed, but only by admitting that the regime could not rule by consent.
However, the stand-off continued: 350,000 attended Popiełuszko's funeral in 1984.
The claim is therefore only partly valid: martial law showed strength to suppress but weakness to solve.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the role of Gorbachev in the collapse of Soviet control over Eastern Europe between 1985 and 1989.

decodeKey.verb: Evaluate: weigh strengths and limits, then judge
decodeKey.judgement: How far Gorbachev, rather than other forces, ended Soviet control

modelPlan.thesis: Gorbachev's role was decisive because he removed the threat of Soviet force, publicly in December 1988; but Afghanistan and economic collapse had already narrowed his options, and the revolutions were made by Eastern Europeans.
modelPlan.counter: The US played little part, Judt says, so the outcome was decided inside the bloc, by both Gorbachev and the peoples.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Would the revolutions have succeeded without Gorbachev? The record of 1953, 1956, 1968 and 1981 suggests not.

segments.text: Gorbachev's role was decisive because he removed the threat of Soviet force.
He abandoned the Brezhnev Doctrine and told the UN on 7 December 1988 that 'Freedom of choice is a universal principle. There should be no exceptions.'
This meant that the regimes lost their final guarantee, so in 1989 Poland and Hungary negotiated while East Germany and Czechoslovakia collapsed.
However, Afghanistan had already made force in Eastern Europe unthinkable, and the revolutions were made by Eastern Europeans themselves.
Gorbachev's role was therefore decisive in removing the barrier, while others made the revolutions.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the causes and consequences of the declaration of martial law in Poland in 1981.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.judgement: Which cause mattered most, and which consequence was most significant

modelPlan.thesis: Martial law was declared because economic collapse and Solidarity's power made Moscow fear the regime was losing control; its main consequence was a stand-off between state and society that repression could not resolve.

arguments.claim: Cause: Soviet pressure for firm action.

modelPlan.counter: Martial law may have prevented a Soviet invasion, as Jaruzelski claimed.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which consequence lasted longest? The stand-off, which ended only with the Round Table of 1989.

segments.text: Martial law was declared mainly because Moscow and Warsaw feared the regime was losing control.
In 1981 industrial productivity collapsed, and on 13 December Jaruzelski, with Soviet encouragement, imprisoned Solidarity's leaders.
This meant that opposition was suppressed, but the economy did not recover, so by 1984 Poland faced a stand-off between society and state.
However, Jaruzelski claimed martial law forestalled a Soviet invasion, which would have been far worse.
Its most significant consequence was therefore a stand-off that only negotiation in 1989 could end.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the Soviet response to the Polish crisis of 1981 and to the revolutions of 1989.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, explicitly linked

modelPlan.thesis: In both crises the Soviet army stayed out, but in 1981 Moscow encouraged martial law to crush Solidarity, whereas in 1989 it renounced force and let the regimes fall, because Afghanistan and Gorbachev's priorities had ended the Brezhnev Doctrine.

arguments.claim: Similarity: no Soviet invasion in either.
Difference: encouragement of force against renunciation.

modelPlan.counter: In both cases the Polish regime itself, under Jaruzelski, chose how to respond.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which difference mattered most? Moscow's attitude to force.

segments.text: In both 1981 and 1989 the Soviet army stayed out of Poland, but Moscow's attitude to force was opposite.
In 1981 the Soviet leadership encouraged Jaruzelski's martial law, whereas in December 1988 Gorbachev told the UN that 'freedom of choice' had no exceptions.
This meant that in 1981 the regime could crush Solidarity, but in 1989 it had to negotiate, so Solidarity won the elections of 4 June.
However, the underlying problems were the same: debt and economic failure, which had grown worse by 1989.
The decisive difference was therefore Soviet policy, shaped by Afghanistan and Gorbachev's priorities.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the reasons why the revolutions of 1989 in Eastern Europe were mostly peaceful.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.judgement: Which reason mattered most, and how they connect

modelPlan.thesis: The revolutions were mostly peaceful because Moscow would not intervene, regimes in Poland and Hungary chose to negotiate, and opposition movements had long avoided confrontation; Romania, where the leader refused reform, was the exception.
modelPlan.counter: The collapse of the East German regime was sudden rather than negotiated, yet still peaceful.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which reason mattered most? Soviet restraint, without which regimes might have chosen force.

segments.text: The revolutions of 1989 were mostly peaceful mainly because the Soviet Union would not intervene.
Gorbachev had abandoned the Brezhnev Doctrine, and in Poland the Round Table led to Solidarity's victory on 4 June and a non-Communist Prime Minister by 24 August.
This meant that regimes without Soviet backing chose to negotiate, and opposition leaders, who had long rejected open confrontation, met them halfway.
However, in Romania Ceauşescu refused reform and his forces fired on crowds, so peace depended on each regime's choices.
Soviet restraint was therefore the main reason, while negotiation and self-limitation explain how change happened.
